title: Nero's fire
hook: Christians were blamed for the fire of Rome and killed as entertainment

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter and Paul in Rome, Cephas among them: the fisherman and the tentmaker, one city, one feast. Your line was the rock and the tentmaker. Did you find a kind word for someone you argue with? Day six hundred ninety-nine.

The man who tells this story didn't like Christians. Tacitus was a Roman senator and historian, and he called their faith a harmful superstition. Yet his history of the emperors is where we read what happened to them. A fire broke out in Rome and raged through the city, burning whole districts. Afterward a rumor would not die: that the emperor Nero had wanted the fire. Relief for the homeless didn't stop it. Prayers to the gods didn't stop it. Nero needed somebody else to blame.
screen: `A HISTORIAN WHO DIDN'T LIKE THEM.` → `ROME BURNS.` → `A RUMOR THAT WON'T DIE.`

segments.voice: Here's what Tacitus says happened next, in his Annals. To get rid of the rumor, Nero fastened the guilt on a group the crowd already hated, people called Christians. Tacitus even explains the name: it came from Christus, who had been executed under Tiberius by the governor Pontius Pilate. First those who confessed were arrested. Then, on what they disclosed, a great crowd of others, convicted, Tacitus says, not so much of setting the fire as of hatred of the human race. Second, the killing was a show. Some were dressed in the skins of animals and torn apart by dogs. Some were nailed to crosses. Some were set alight to serve as torches when daylight was gone. Nero opened his own gardens for it and mingled with the crowd. Third, the surprising turn, from the man who disliked them. Tacitus still calls them guilty people who deserved the harshest punishment. Yet he writes that a feeling of pity rose for them, because they were being destroyed not for the public good, but to feed one man's cruelty. Fourth, what the Church remembers. Nobody knows these martyrs' names. The Catholic calendar keeps a memorial for them anyway, the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, placed beside the feast of Peter and Paul. And their story echoes a line from the First Letter of Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name." Scapegoating didn't end in Rome. When a city is afraid, a crowd still looks for someone to carry the fear: a minority, a newcomer, a neighbor who is different. The carry names what happened to these Christians so it can be recognized when it happens to anyone.
screen: `NERO FASTENS THE GUILT.` · `KILLED AS A SHOW.` · `PITY FROM A CRITIC.` · `MARTYRS WITH NO NAMES.` · then, large: `LET HIM NOT BE ASHAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember anyone who is being blamed for what they didn't do. Settle, and breathe. It might be a group in the news, a kid at school, a coworker everyone talks about when he leaves the room. Maybe it's someone you've blamed yourself. Don't argue the case. Just let them stand there in your mind as a person, not a target. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for the people doing the blaming. If you don't, hold them in plain attention. The bell holds the time.
Nero's fire. The burning of Rome, and the Christians the emperor blamed for it and killed as a public show. Today's word.
Your line: blamed for the fire. Today, when you hear a whole group blamed for something, ask who actually did it. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: The Catholic calendar keeps a memorial for the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, killed under Nero, and Catholics often pray for persecuted people at Mass in the prayers of the faithful.

it comes from Tacitus, a Roman historian who disliked Christians.
Tacitus says they were convicted mainly of arson
he says less for the fire than for hatred of the human race.
he says Christus was executed by Pilate under Tiberius.

fork.setup: you're Nero. Rome has burned. relief and prayers to the gods haven't stopped the rumor that you wanted the fire. what do you do?
options: admit the rumor and step down.
find a hated group to blame.
ignore it and wait for it to pass.
fork.reveal: Tacitus says Nero fastened the guilt on Christians. Tacitus, who thought them guilty all the same, says people came to pity them.

trapdoor: what you thought: Christians in Rome were killed for setting the fire.
what it means: Nero blamed a group the crowd already hated, to turn a rumor away from himself.
what a scholar hears: Annals 15.44, a Roman source outside the Church naming Christus and Pilate, written by a man with no love for Christians.

notes: 1 Peter 4:16 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording: confirm exact text.

Tacitus Annals 15.44 paraphrased throughout (no public-domain translation on the approved list); 'harmful superstition' paraphrases exitiabilis superstitio. Confirm the paraphrase of 'hatred of the human race' (odio humani generis) and of the pity passage.
The memorial of the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church (30 June) is described as 'placed beside the feast of Peter and Paul' without a date. Confirm.
Whether Nero set the fire is not settled; script reports only that Tacitus records the rumor.
Tacitus says the fire lasted several days; script avoids the count.

Editor: Tacitus's pity passage now keeps his own judgment that the Christians deserved punishment (Annals 15.44), so he is not made to sound sympathetic; cut 'Even their critic could see what a scapegoat was'; arrest sequence follows the text (those who confessed first).
